title: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick took a softer line on Nvidia as calls for tougher controls grew.
text:
Nvidia Earnings and Forecasts Beat Expectations
The earnings report covered a period before the resignation of its chief executive Jensen Huang. The board chair said there were no plans to bring back Mr. Huang, who earlier Tuesday said he would be open to returning.
Nvidia’s stock price this year
Latest
Nvidia reported on Tuesday that its quarterly sales topped $100 billion for the first time, more than twice as much as a year earlier, in what may amount to the final testament of the artificial intelligence company’s breakneck growth under its ousted chief executive Jensen Huang.
Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion and profit of $65.3 billion in the three months ending in October. Both figures exceeded Wall Street’s expectations, and pushed the company’s stock price higher in after-hours trading. The figures, which cut against concerns about a growth slowdown in the artificial intelligence industry, and with it a slowdown in profits, were a relief for investors. Nvidia projected revenue in the current quarter to be even larger, about $130 billion, suggesting that it is still growing rapidly.
The earnings report came a week after Mr. Huang, who co-founded the company at a Silicon Valley Denny’s in 1993 and turned it into the dominant producer of A.I. chips, resigned as chief executive. His exit followed revelations that he had two relationships that violated the company’s code of conduct, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing. He also misled the company’s board of directors.
Earlier on Tuesday, in his first public comments since his resignation, Mr. Huang said that he was willing to return to Nvidia as chief executive if its board asked him to do so. But Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, ruled that out in a call with investors and analysts.
Mr. Jones said Mr. Huang voluntarily resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive after “personal behavior inconsistent with its code of conduct,” and that the board of directors had unanimously accepted that resignation. He said the board had no plan to reinstate Mr. Huang.
During the call, Nvidia said it would stop shipping its chips to China. Mr. Huang had fought for months to get U.S. government approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chip, an older generation product, to Chinese companies. To win approval, he cut a deal with President Trump to give the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of sales to China.
But China hasn’t shown much interest in buying them. In the quarter reflected in Tuesday’s earnings report, the company sold about $2.4 billion in chips to China, a fraction of the company’s $115.8 billion in total revenue for the period.
Nvidia’s staggering business growth now faces the biggest test in the company’s history after Mr. Huang’s exit. The fallout has yet to be fully felt, but it has already reverberated from Silicon Valley to Beijing and Washington, where officials are pushing new restrictions on sales of chips that have powered the A.I. boom.
“Our momentum is real,” said Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, to conclude the investor call. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”
Here’s what else to know:
- Interim C.E.O.: Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, is serving as Nvidia’s interim chief executive. Nvidia said it had hired a search firm to find a new leader and would be proceeding with an independent investigation into Mr. Huang’s affair with the Chinese businesswoman.
- Singular leader: Mr. Huang ran a company with a flat organizational structure where he had over 60 direct reports. He was the company’s chief technologist, chief sales officer and top lobbyist in Washington, where had become a close ally of President Trump’s. He had no obvious successor.
- A.I. rules: New U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips could jeopardize billions in investment in Southeast Asia and force countries in the region to strike an increasingly difficult balance between Washington and Beijing. Read more ›
- Asia trip: The fallout from Mr. Huang’s resignation is lingering over Mr. Trump’s trip to China this week. Mr. Huang has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, and Mr. Trump has sought to downplay Chinese efforts to spy on Mr. Huang. Read more ›
Nvidia shares were up 4 percent in after-hours trading. It was an encouraging sign for a beleaguered company that had a market value flirting with $6 trillion a month ago. In the wake of all that has happened — reports about Huang being targeted by Chinese intelligence, news of relationships with a customer and an employee, Huang’s resignation, and new rules restricting sales of chips to Southeast Asia — Nvidia is valued at $3.75 trillion.
Gina Raimondo, the former commerce secretary, spent a lot of time with Jensen Huang, and he wasn’t always happy.
Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference on Tuesday, Raimondo said the Biden administration put national security first and clearly defined what Nvidia and other chip sellers could and couldn’t sell to China.
“This administration hasn’t been like that,” Raimondo said. Instead, she said the Trump administration has been continually shifting its position from preventing sales to allowing sales to taking a 25 percent cut of sales.
“You’re either for America’s national security or you’re not — it’s not at a price,” Raimondo said.
The anatomy of the Nvidia scandal
Nvidia’s earnings aren’t the only marquee event for the A.I. industry this week. Today’s results are likely to set a more stable stage for Anthropic to launch its initial public offering tomorrow, with trading in the new public stock to start on Thursday. A tailwind in the market for other A.I. stocks should help investor sentiment for Anthropic.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.
Speaking at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Lisa Su, the chief executive of AMD, Nvidia’s largest rival, said that people watching Jensen Huang’s effort should separate “from the noise,” which will “work itself out in time.”
“Jensen has been a tremendous leader for the industry,” she said.
Her remarks speak to a concern rippling across the industry. Over the past three years, Huang has become the chip industry’s biggest cheerleader, helping breath life into the oldest segment of Silicon Valley. Everyone is wondering what a future looks like without him.
For investors, that went about as well as it could have. Strong earnings for the third quarter that beat expectations. Strong guidance for the fourth quarter that beat expectations. And strong guidance through next year, rebuffing concerns that the company was set for a slowdown in 2027. Nvidia’s stock price is higher. Its rivals stock prices are higher. This is likely to now ripple through markets overnight.
President Trump called Jensen Huang last week, before the Nvidia chief stepped down Thursday amid a rapidly unfolding spy scandal, and urged him to keep fighting for his job, according to two people briefed on the conversation.
The call was the latest instance of Mr. Trump defending and protecting Mr. Huang, who had become a high-profile ally and an influential adviser on artificial intelligence. The president continued to back him to the end, even after U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Mr. Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
Nvidia announced on Thursday that Mr. Huang, who built the company into the world’s leading supplier of advanced A.I. chips, had been replaced as chief executive following revelations not just of the affair with the woman suspected of being a spy, but also another with one of his employees.
A representative for Mr. Huang did not provide a comment for this article. Neither Mr. Trump nor the White House responded to requests for comment about his call to Mr. Huang.
The president had been warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a Chinese citizen known as Alice Huang, who intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.
Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”
Colette Kress, the interim chief executive, signed off the call 10 minutes ahead of schedule with no more questions remaining.
“Our momentum is real,” she said. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”
When asked about what the changing political landscape means for Nvidia, Kress said that it was important companies work together so that communities understand the opportunities that come with data centers, including jobs and tax revenue.
“The demand and what we have in terms of agentic will continue,” she said, not only in 2027 but in 2028, as well.
Some Democrats elected in the midterm election have vowed to halt data center development and rein in A.I. companies.
An analyst asked about margin forecasts. “Is there an acceptable rate of margin compression that you could live with?” the analyst asks. Kress said “we feel confident” about keeping margins high.
Margins are important because if they fall, profit growth could also still fall even if demand for Nvidia’s chips kept growing. While the company would be selling more of its products, it would be profiting less from each sale. Kress communicated confidence that the company will retain pricing power.
Kress said the leadership of TSMC, the premier chip producer, was in Nvidia’s offices this week and was “fully engaged in helping us.” TSMC, a Taiwanese company that produces about 90 percent of the world’s most advanced chips, is one of Nvidia’s most important business partners.
Huang has previously said Nvidia’s business with TSMC was built on his handshake agreements with its leadership. Kress has told investors that the relationship is continuing even without Huang.
The Nvidia board chairman, Harvey C. Jones, said the company is looking at external and internal candidates for chief executive.
“The search will be thorough,” he said. “We want to install the C.E.O., the permanent C.E.O., as quickly as possible.” He added they won’t expedite the search “before finding exactly the right person.”
Colette Kress said that the company is making employees a priority during this period of leadership transition. “Like every community that’s out there, there are diverse opinions,” she said. “Our employees, though, we believe are committed.”
Kress said the company’s leadership has stood up over the past week to prepare for earnings and support employees around the world. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world class roadmap,” she said. “It’s business as usual.”
Gross profit margins are expected to hold above 70 percent, Kress said. Investors have worried that competition will bring down the cost of Nvidia’s chips, lowering these margins. Ms. Kress’s confidence in keeping them up is indicative of expectations that continued demand will allow prices for those chips to remain high.
Ian Buck is joining Colette Kress and Harvey C. Jones on the question-and-answer section of Nvidia’s calls with investors. Buck is a vice president at Nvidia and the inventor of Cuda, a software that allows Nvidia’s chips to be used to train A.I. He is now considered by some to be a front-runner to permanently succeed Huang.
Nvidia’s call with Wall Street analysts today has offered Colette Kress, the company’s interim chief executive, her first chance to speak about the events of the past week. Kress has served as the company’s chief financial officer since joining Nvidia in 2013. She has a bachelor’s degree in finance from the University of Arizona and a master’s degree in business administration from Southern Methodist University. She previously worked in finance at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco, before joining Nvidia in 2013. Huang interviewed 22 candidates before hiring Kress as chief financial officer.
Harvey C. Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, joined the interim chief executive Colette Kress on the company’s call with investors. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, the year it was founded, and was previously the chief executive of Synopsys, an early business partner of Nvidia that provided software for designing chips.
Madison Huang was yelling. Her father, Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been scheduled to headline a conference in New Delhi in February. Shortly before the event, Mr. Huang pulled out and tapped a longtime lieutenant, Jay Puri, to attend in his place.
But Nvidia hadn’t buttoned up its plans for the conference, infuriating Ms. Huang. On a call ahead of the event, Ms. Huang berated other employees — including Mr. Puri — for being unprepared. Eventually, Mr. Puri interrupted and told Ms. Huang he could answer her questions if she stopped yelling at him. Less than six months later, he left his role at Nvidia.
The tense meeting highlighted the powerful and sometimes disruptive role Ms. Huang, 35, played at the company her father co-founded, according to more than a dozen current and former employees who spoke on condition of anonymity about the family’s leadership of Nvidia. Before Mr. Huang resigned last week, she had become his de facto chief of staff, with considerable authority over more seasoned executives.
That influence has created an immediate challenge for Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, who replaced Mr. Huang after his resignation last week. Ms. Kress must quickly determine how much power Ms. Huang will have in the company after her father’s exit.
She also must assess and address concerns among senior executives that Ms. Huang has conflicted loyalties between the company and her father, who has President Trump’s support in efforts to return to Nvidia.
Nvidia said it will stop shipping H200 chips to China. Those are the only chips the company can legally sell to China. Jensen Huang fought for months to get permission to sell them to China and struck a deal with President Trump to give the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of sales. But China hasn’t shown much interest in buying them. In the October quarter, the company sold about $2.4 billion in chips to China, a fraction of the company’s $115.8 billion in total revenue for the period.
Jensen Huang was agitated.
It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her.
Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said.
Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller.
They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship.
Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency.
But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions.
The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret.
On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him.
Nvidia’s board of directors soon convened an emergency meeting to discuss Mr. Huang’s future with his company. Still, it was unimaginable to think of Nvidia without him.
Less than 24 hours later, Mr. Huang resigned.
